title: Vanderbilt Team Builds AI Agent to Fast-Track Alzheimer's Treatment Referrals
excerpt: An adaptive AI system aims to close the gap between new disease-modifying drugs and the primary care bottleneck that leaves most eligible patients undiagnosed.
body:
• Researchers at Vanderbilt University Medical Center have developed an AI agent that can accelerate Alzheimer's diagnosis and treatment by automating the referral process from primary care to specialist dementia clinics.
  • The system uses an adaptive cascading AI framework that screens patients at multiple stages, reducing the time and cost of identifying candidates for treatment with new anti-amyloid drugs like lecanemab and donanemab.
  • Currently, primary care physicians identify fewer than half of eligible Alzheimer's patients for specialist referral, creating a critical bottleneck as new disease-modifying treatments become available.
  • The AI tool is designed to work within existing clinical workflows, flagging high-risk patients for cognitive assessment and fast-tracking referrals without requiring expensive PET scans or spinal taps for initial screening.

A Bottleneck in Dementia Care

The arrival of disease-modifying Alzheimer's drugs — lecanemab and donanemab — has created an unexpected problem. For the first time, doctors have treatments that can slow cognitive decline in early-stage patients. But the infrastructure to identify and refer those patients simply does not exist at scale.

Primary care physicians, who see the vast majority of older adults, identify fewer than half of patients who might benefit from specialist evaluation. The reasons are straightforward: cognitive screening takes time, referral pathways are fragmented, and dementia specialists are in short supply. The result is that many patients who could benefit from early treatment are never assessed.

How the AI Agent Works

A team at Vanderbilt University Medical Center has built an AI agent designed to close this gap. Published in Nature and detailed in a companion paper in Springer Nature Link, the system uses what researchers call an "adaptive cascading" approach — a multi-stage screening process that progressively narrows the pool of patients who need specialist attention.

At the first stage, the AI analyzes electronic health records to flag patients with risk factors and early indicators of cognitive decline. Those flagged patients receive a more detailed automated assessment. Only those who pass both filters are referred to a specialist, reducing the burden on both primary care physicians and dementia clinics while ensuring that high-risk patients are not missed.

The key innovation is that the system works within existing clinical workflows. It does not require expensive PET scans or cerebrospinal fluid analysis for initial screening — tests that cost thousands of dollars and are available only at specialized centers. Instead, it uses data already in the patient's medical record, combined with brief cognitive assessments that can be administered in a standard office visit.

Why Speed Matters

Anti-amyloid drugs work best in the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease, before significant neuronal damage has occurred. Every month of delay in diagnosis is a month of potential treatment lost. The Vanderbilt team's modeling suggests their AI system could cut the average time from initial symptom recognition to specialist referral by several months — a meaningful improvement for a disease where the treatment window is narrow.

"The goal is straightforward: to ensure that patients who could benefit from new treatments are identified and referred before their disease progresses beyond the point where those treatments can help."

— Vanderbilt University Medical Center research team

Scaling the Solution

The challenge now is deployment. The AI system needs to be integrated into electronic health record platforms used by primary care practices — a process that involves regulatory approvals, clinical validation, and physician training. The Vanderbilt team is working with health systems to pilot the technology, with broader rollout expected as anti-amyloid drugs become more widely prescribed.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications extend beyond the U.S. healthcare system. India has an estimated 8.8 million people living with dementia, a number projected to reach 17 million by 2036. AI-driven screening tools developed for Western health systems could eventually be adapted for Indian clinical settings, where the specialist shortage is even more acute. The gap between treatment availability and diagnostic capacity is a global problem — and AI may be the most scalable solution available.
